tenseOptions.label: Present
tenseOptions.title: Present (presente)
tenseOptions.description: Current or habitual actions: parlo = I speak / I am speaking.

tenseOptions.label: Passato prossimo
tenseOptions.title: Passato prossimo (present perfect)
tenseOptions.description: Completed actions: avere or essere + past participle. With essere the participle agrees with the subject (andato / andata).

tenseOptions.label: Imperfect
tenseOptions.title: Imperfetto (imperfect)
tenseOptions.description: Ongoing or habitual past actions: parlavo = I was speaking / I used to speak.

tenseOptions.label: Future
tenseOptions.title: Futuro semplice (future)
tenseOptions.description: Future actions: parlerò = I will speak.

tenseOptions.label: Conditional
tenseOptions.title: Condizionale presente (conditional)
tenseOptions.description: Polite requests and hypotheticals: vorrei = I would like.

functions.label: Ability / permission
functions.description: Can, cannot, may: potere (posso, puoi), sapere for a learned skill (so nuotare), riuscire a for managing to do something.

functions.label: Necessity / need
functions.description: Have to and need to: dovere (devo, dobbiamo) or avere bisogno di.

functions.label: Desire / wish
functions.description: Want, would like, hope: volere (voglio), the conditional vorrei / mi piacerebbe, desiderare, sperare di.

functions.label: Used to / was
functions.description: Ongoing or habitual past in the imperfetto: ero, avevo, abitavo, facevo.

functions.label: Future plans
functions.description: Plans and intentions: the futuro (andrò, farò) or avere intenzione di.

functions.label: Likes / preferences
functions.description: Likes and preferences: mi piace / mi piacciono, preferire.

functions.label: Prepositions
functions.description: Where, when, with whom: a with cities and times (a Roma, alle otto), in with countries, rooms and transport (in Italia, in treno), da for origin, someone's place or "since" (da Marco, da due anni), di for origin and possession. Joined with the article: a + il = al, in + la = nella, su + il = sul.

sentenceTypes.label: Negative
sentenceTypes.description: A sentence with non or nessuno.

sentenceTypes.label: Request / command
sentenceTypes.description: Asks or tells someone to do something, or orders (Vorrei..., Giri a destra).

steps.text: Saying hello
Italians choose a greeting based on two things: the time of day, and how well they know you. Let’s start with the one you probably already know.

steps.note: Casual: friends, family, children and people your own age. It works for hello and for goodbye.
The polite, all-purpose hello from morning until early afternoon. Use it in shops and cafés, and with anyone you don’t know.
Takes over from *buongiorno* in the late afternoon, from around 4 or 5 pm.
A neutral hello, useful when you can’t decide between casual and polite.
Often added to a polite greeting. Before a surname, *signore* shortens to *signor*: *Buongiorno, signor Rossi!*

steps.label: Tu or Lei?
steps.text: Italian has two words for “you”. *Tu* is casual: friends, family, children, people your age. *Lei* is polite: strangers, shop staff, older people. *Ciao* goes with *tu*; *buongiorno* and *buonasera* are safe with anyone.

steps.prompt: It’s 10 am and you walk into a bakery. What do you say?
steps.why: You don’t know the baker, so be polite, and it’s morning, so *buongiorno*.

steps.prompt: You bump into a friend from class at 7 pm. What’s the most natural greeting?
steps.why: With a friend, *ciao* is natural at any hour.

steps.text: Saying goodbye

steps.note: The standard goodbye. Polite enough for anyone, and friends use it too.
What shop staff say as you leave during the day. In the evening it becomes *buona serata*.
Only for the end of the night, when someone is going home or to bed. Never use it as a greeting.

steps.prompt: You’re leaving a friend’s place at midnight. What do you say?
steps.why: *Buonanotte* is for the end of the night. *Salve* is only a hello.

steps.prompt: Which goodbye can you use with anyone, casual or polite?
steps.why: *Arrivederci* works everywhere. *Ciao* is only for people you’d call *tu*.

steps.text: In conversation
Anna stops at a café on her way to work. Tap any line to hear it again.

lines.narration: Anna drinks her coffee and pays.

steps.text: That evening, Anna runs into her friend Luca.

lines.en: Good night, Anna! See you tomorrow!

lessons.title: Mi chiamo…
lessons.subtitle: Introducing yourself
goals: Say your name and ask someone theirs
Respond when you meet someone new

steps.text: What’s your name?
Italians don’t say “my name is”. They say *mi chiamo*, literally “I call myself”. Learn it as one block for now. The grammar behind it comes much later.

steps.note: Literally “How do you call yourself?” Use it with people you’d greet with *ciao*.
The *Lei* version, for strangers and older people. It also means “What’s he / she called?”
The quick way: *Sono Marco*, “I’m Marco.”
Polite version: *E Lei?*

steps.prompt: A new classmate says *Ciao, mi chiamo Sara.* What is she telling you?
steps.why: *Mi chiamo Sara* means “My name is Sara.”

steps.prompt: You’re asking an elderly gentleman his name. Which question do you use?
steps.why: With a stranger or someone older, use the polite *Lei* form: *Come si chiama?*

steps.text: Nice to meet you

steps.note: Said with a handshake, often with your name: *Piacere, Marco.*
A friendly reply to *piacere*. You can also just say *piacere* back.

steps.label: Culture
steps.text: Italians shake hands when they meet someone new, and friends often greet each other with a kiss on each cheek. Either way, *piacere* is the word that goes with it.
Where are you from?

steps.note: Polite version: *Di dov’è?*
Use it with a city: *Sono di Roma*, *Sono di Chicago*. For countries you’ll use a nationality instead, which is in lesson 5.

steps.label: Tip
steps.text: *Io* means “I”. Italian usually drops it, because *sono* already tells you who is speaking. Add it for contrast: *Lui è di Roma, io sono di Napoli*, “He’s from Rome, I’m from Naples.”

steps.prompt: Someone asks *Di dove sei?* Which answer fits?
steps.why: *Di dove sei?* asks where you’re from, so *Sono di Torino*, “I’m from Turin.”

steps.prompt: Someone shakes your hand and says *Piacere!* What’s a natural reply?

steps.text: In conversation
At a friend’s party, Marco meets Emma. They’re about the same age, so they use *tu*.

lines.it: Ciao! Mi chiamo Marco. E tu?
lines.en: Hi! My name’s Marco. And you?
Hi, I’m Emma. Nice to meet you!
The pleasure’s mine! Where are you from?

steps.text: Now a polite version. Two strangers meet at a conference, so they use *Lei*.

lines.en: Good morning. My name is Giorgio Rossi.
Nice to meet you, Paola Bianchi.
Very nice to meet you. Where are you from, ma’am?

lessons.title: Come stai?
lessons.subtitle: How are you?
goals: Ask how someone is, casually and politely
Answer honestly, from great to not so good
Keep the conversation going with *e tu?*

steps.text: How are you?
After hello, Italians usually ask how you are, and unlike in English, they may actually expect an answer.

steps.note: From the verb *stare*. Use it with anyone you’d call *tu*.
The *Lei* version, for people you’d greet with *buongiorno*.
Relaxed and very common. It works with both *tu* and *Lei*.

steps.label: Grammar in a nutshell
steps.text: Italian has two verbs for “to be”: *essere* and *stare*. For how you feel, Italians use *stare*: *sto bene* means “I’m well”. For now, just learn *sto* as the word that goes with how you are.
Answering

steps.title: From great to not so good

steps.note: The full sentence. Often shortened to just *bene*.
Tag it on after your answer: *Bene, grazie.*
Throw the question back.
Short for *anche io*. *Bene anch’io* means “I’m well too.”
Tired uses *essere*, not *stare*. The ending matches you: *stanco* for a man, *stanca* for a woman.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks *Come stai?* and you feel great. What do you say?
Your new neighbour is an older woman. How do you ask how she is?
steps.why: *Come sta?* is the polite *Lei* form.

steps.label: Culture
steps.text: Italians answer “how are you?” more honestly than English speakers do. Saying *così così* or *non c’è male* is perfectly normal, and may start a real chat.
In conversation
Giulia meets her friend Paolo at the bus stop.
Later, Giulia meets her elderly neighbour, Signora Conti, on the stairs.

lines.en: Good morning, Mrs Conti! How are you?

lines.it: Non c’è male, grazie. E tu, cara?
lines.en: Not bad, thanks. And you, dear?

steps.label: Notice
steps.text: Signora Conti says *tu* to Giulia, but Giulia says *Lei* to her. Older people often use *tu* with younger ones, while the younger person stays polite until invited to switch.

lessons.title: Per favore, grazie
lessons.subtitle: Polite essentials
goals: Say please, thank you and you’re welcome

steps.text: Please and thank you

steps.note: Goes at the end of a request: *Un caffè, per favore.*
*Grazie mille* is literally “a thousand thanks”.
It also means “please, go ahead”: when holding a door, inviting someone in, or handing something over.
A casual alternative to *prego*.

steps.label: Culture
steps.text: *Prego* is one of the most useful words in Italian. A waiter who says *Prego?* means “What can I get you?”. A shopkeeper handing you your change says *prego*. So does someone waving you through a door.
Excuse me and sorry

steps.note: To get someone’s attention, or to apologise for something small. *Scusi* for strangers, *scusa* for friends.

steps.en: Excuse me, where is the pharmacy?

steps.note: For squeezing past people on a crowded bus, or when stepping into someone’s home.
Real regret or sympathy: bad news, or when you can’t help. Bumping into someone is *scusi*, not *mi dispiace*.

steps.prompt: You need to get past people blocking the train door. You say:
steps.why: *Permesso* is “coming through”.

steps.prompt: You step on a stranger’s foot. You say:
steps.why: A stranger gets the polite *scusi*. *Scusa* is for friends.

steps.text: When you don’t understand

steps.note: Casual version: *Puoi ripetere?*
Casual version: *Parli inglese?*

steps.it: Scusi, non capisco. Può ripetere, per favore?
steps.en: Sorry, I don’t understand. Can you repeat that, please?

steps.prompt: A stranger asks you for directions, but you’re a tourist and have no idea. You say:
steps.why: You’re sorry you can’t help, so *mi dispiace*.

steps.prompt: Someone is speaking too fast for you. What do you ask?

steps.text: In conversation
Tom, a tourist, is lost in Rome and looking for *la stazione*, the station. He stops a passer-by.

lines.en: Excuse me, ma’am! Do you speak English?

lines.it: È a destra, dopo la piazza.
lines.en: It’s on the right, after the square.

lines.it: Scusi, non capisco. Può ripetere, per favore?
lines.en: Sorry, I don’t understand. Can you repeat that, please?
On the right. After the square.

lessons.title: Io sono…
lessons.subtitle: The verb essere
goals: Use all six forms of *essere* (to be)
Say your nationality with the right ending
Make a sentence negative with *non*, and ask yes / no questions

steps.text: To be: essere
*Essere* (to be) is the most common verb in Italian, and like “to be” in English, it’s irregular. You’ve already met *sono*. Here is the whole family.

steps.label: Watch out
steps.text: *Sono* means both “I am” and “they are”. The context tells you which. Also, *è* (is) has an accent, while *e* without one means “and”.

steps.label: Tip
steps.text: The polite *Lei* uses the same form as “he / she”: *Lei è italiana?* can mean “Is she Italian?” or, to a woman, “Are you Italian?”. Context, and the capital L in writing, tell you which. The adjective still matches the person you’re talking to: a man is asked *Lei è italiano?*

steps.prompt: Complete: *Tu ___ di Roma?* (Are you from Rome?)

steps.text: Nationalities
Nationality words describe you, so their ending matches you. Most end in *-o* for a man and *-a* for a woman.

steps.title: Nationalities with *-e*, the same for everyone

steps.it: Marco è italiano. Giulia è italiana.
steps.en: Marco is Italian. Giulia is Italian.

steps.label: Notice
steps.text: Italian writes nationalities with a small letter: *italiano*, not “Italiano”.
Saying no, and asking
To make a sentence negative, put *non* right before the verb. That’s all there is to it.
To ask a yes / no question, keep the same words and raise your voice at the end.

steps.prompt: Emma is from London. How does she say “I’m not Italian”?
steps.why: *Non* goes before the verb, and Emma is a woman, so *italiana*.

steps.prompt: Pedro is from Madrid. Which sentence is right?

steps.text: In conversation
At a language exchange in Florence, Chiara meets two newcomers, Sam and Mia.

lines.it: No, non sono di Toronto. Sono di Vancouver.
lines.en: No, I’m not from Toronto. I’m from Vancouver.

lessons.title: Numeri e anni
lessons.subtitle: Numbers 0–20 and age
goals: Ask someone’s age and give yours

steps.text: 0 to 10

steps.title: Tap a number to hear it

steps.label: Tip
steps.text: *Sei* is both “six” and “you are” (from *essere*). Context always tells you which.
Eleven to sixteen end in *-dici*, from *dieci* (ten). Seventeen to nineteen flip it around, and *dici-* comes first.

steps.title: Tap a number to hear it

steps.label: Pattern
steps.text: Compare *sedici* (16, “six-ten”) with *diciassette* (17, “ten-seven”). The switch happens at seventeen.
How old are you?
In English you are an age. In Italian you have years, so age uses *avere* (to have), not *essere*.

steps.label: Spelling
steps.text: The h in *ho*, *hai* and *ha* is silent. It’s there to tell *ho* (I have) apart from *o* (or), and *ha* (has) from *a* (to).

steps.note: Literally “How many years do you have?” Polite version: *Quanti anni ha?*
Always include *anni*: *Ho diciotto anni.*

steps.why: Age uses *avere*, and *ho* is “I have”. *Ha* would be “he / she has”.

steps.text: In conversation
At summer camp, Alessia, a counsellor, chats with a new camper.

lines.narration: Luca points at a girl nearby.

lines.en: And her? How old is she?

lines.it: Lei è Sofia. Ha dodici anni.

lessons.title: Ripasso 1
lessons.subtitle: Review: meeting someone new
goals: Hold a whole first conversation, from hello to goodbye
Pick *tu* or *Lei* and stay with it

steps.text: Tu or Lei?

Lessons 1–6 gave you two versions of most questions: *tu* for friends, children and people your age, *Lei* for strangers, older people and anyone you’d call *signore* or *signora*. Here they are side by side.

items.it: Come ti chiami? / Come si chiama?
Quanti anni hai? / Quanti anni ha?

steps.label: Tip
steps.text: Polite *Lei* uses the same verb form as *lui / lei*: *Lei è*, *Lei ha*, *Lei sta*. Once you know “he / she”, you know the polite “you”.

steps.prompt: You meet your friend’s grandmother. How do you ask how she is?
steps.why: An older person you’ve just met gets *Lei*: *come sta*.

steps.prompt: A student your age asks *Di dove sei?* You answer and ask back:
steps.why: Keep the register they chose: *tu* gets *e tu?*. And where you’re from uses *essere*: *sono di…*

steps.text: Sono, sto, ho
Three verbs share the work English gives to “to be”. *Essere* says who or what you are, *stare* says how you are, and *avere* gives your age.

steps.why: Age is something you have: *avere*.
How you are uses *stare*.
Emma is a woman, so *stanca*, and tired uses *essere*.

steps.text: Questions and answers
Matching answers to questions is the fastest way to keep a conversation going.

steps.why: The question uses *avere*, and so does the answer.

steps.text: In conversation
A language-exchange evening in Bologna: Italians practise English, visitors practise Italian. Jess, from Chicago, sits down next to Davide.

lines.it: Ciao! Io sono Davide. E tu?

lines.en: Hi, my name’s Jess. Nice to meet you!

lines.it: Piacere mio. Di dove sei, Jess?
lines.en: The pleasure’s mine. Where are you from, Jess?

lines.it: Io sono di Bologna. Quanti anni hai?
lines.en: I’m from Bologna. How old are you?
Me too! How are you, Jess?

lines.it: Bene, grazie. Ma sono molto stanca!
lines.en: Fine, thanks. But I’m very tired!
wrong: Bene, grazie. Ma sono molto stanco!

lines.narration: Davide answers very fast, and Jess doesn’t catch a word.

lines.it: Scusa, non capisco. Più piano, per favore!
lines.en: Sorry, I don’t understand. More slowly, please!
wrong: Scusi, non capisco. Più piano, per favore!

lines.narration: The evening ends and everyone gets up to leave.

steps.text: Later, Jess arrives at her homestay. Her host is an older lady, so it’s *Lei* all the way. One new word: *benvenuta*, “welcome” (to a woman).

lines.en: Yes, I’m Jess. Good evening, ma’am!

lines.it: Piacere, sono la signora Bianchi. Come sta?
lines.en: Nice to meet you, I’m Mrs Bianchi. How are you?

lines.it: Molto piacere. Sto bene, grazie. E Lei?
lines.en: Very nice to meet you. I’m well, thank you. And you?
wrong: Molto piacere. Sto bene, grazie. E tu?
Molto piacere. Sono bene, grazie. E Lei?

lines.en: Well, thank you. Are you English?

lines.it: No, non sono inglese. Sono americana, di Chicago.
lines.en: No, I’m not English. I’m American, from Chicago.
wrong: No, non sono inglese. Sono americano, di Chicago.
No, non ho inglese. Sono americana, di Chicago.

lines.en: Thank you so much, ma’am. Good night!

lessons.title: Al bar
lessons.subtitle: Ordering at a café
goals: Order food and drink at a café

steps.text: Ordering

steps.note: The polite way to ask for anything. Use it as a set phrase for now: lesson 29 explains the grammar.

steps.label: Culture
steps.text: *Un caffè* is an espresso: small, strong and drunk in a minute at the counter. Ask for *un caffè americano* if you want a long coffee. Cappuccino is a breakfast drink, and Italians rarely order one after about 11 am.

steps.note: When a group orders, each person says *per me* + the item: *Per me un tè.*

steps.prompt: The polite way to ask for a croissant:
steps.why: *Voglio* (I want) sounds demanding to a stranger. *Vorrei* is polite. And “please” is *per favore*, not *prego*.

steps.prompt: *Acqua* is feminine and starts with a vowel. “A water” is:
steps.why: A feminine word starting with a vowel takes *un’*, with an apostrophe. Lesson 9 has all the rules.

steps.text: The barista speaks

steps.note: The *prego* from lesson 4, this time as a question.
You’ll hear it every time someone hands you something: *Ecco il cappuccino.*

steps.prompt: The barista asks *Altro?* You have everything you want. You say:

steps.text: Paying

steps.note: For the total. For one thing, ask *Quanto costa?* (How much does it cost?)
It never changes: *un euro, due euro*.

steps.label: Culture
steps.text: In many bars you pay first. Go to the *cassa* (till), say what you want, pay, then hand the *scontrino* to the barista, who makes your order. Standing at the counter costs less than sitting at a table.

steps.prompt: *Panino* is masculine. How do you ask the price of one?

steps.text: In conversation
8 am at a bar in Rome. Marta orders breakfast at the counter.

lines.en: Good morning! What can I get you?

lines.it: Buongiorno! Vorrei un cappuccino, per favore.
lines.en: Good morning! I’d like a cappuccino, please.
Here you are. Thanks, have a good day!
Thank you! Have a good day!

steps.text: Later, Luca and Sara stop for a break. Listen for *per me* and *per te* (for you).

lines.en: Hi, guys! What can I get you?

lines.it: Per me un caffè. E per te, Sara?
lines.en: A coffee for me. And for you, Sara?

lines.it: Per me un tè, per favore.
wrong: Per te un tè, per favore.
Per me una tè, per favore.

lessons.title: Il, la, lo
lessons.subtitle: Gender and articles
goals: Guess a noun’s gender from its ending

steps.text: Masculine or feminine?
Every Italian noun is masculine or feminine, even a table or a phone. The ending usually tells you which.

steps.label: Exceptions
steps.text: A few common words break the pattern: *la mano* (the hand) is feminine and *il problema* (the problem) is masculine. Words borrowed from English, like *lo sport* and *il bar*, are usually masculine.

steps.why: It ends in *-o*.

steps.text: The: il, lo, la, l’

steps.label: Why lo?
steps.text: *Lo* makes words easier to say: *il zaino* catches on the tongue, *lo zaino* flows. It’s used before *z*, *s* + consonant, *gn* and *ps* (*lo psicologo*). *L’* does the same job before vowels: *la acqua* becomes *l’acqua*.

steps.why: A masculine noun starting with *z* takes *lo*.
*S* + consonant (*st-*) takes *lo*.

steps.text: A, an: un, uno, una, un’

steps.label: Pattern
steps.text: Masculine nouns take *un*, except the *lo* words, which take *uno*. The apostrophe only appears in the feminine: *un amico* (no apostrophe), *un’amica* (apostrophe).

steps.why: Feminine + vowel: *un’*, with the apostrophe. Without it, *un amica* would look masculine.
The masculine never takes the apostrophe.

steps.label: Tip
steps.text: Learn every noun with its article: not *zaino* but *lo zaino*. The Nouns tab drills exactly this.
In conversation
Giulia’s little brother Matteo is leaving on a school trip. She checks his bag before he goes.

lines.en: Matteo, have you got your backpack?

lines.it: Hai un libro per il treno?
lines.en: Have you got a book for the train?
wrong: Hai uno libro per il treno?
Hai una libro per il treno?

lines.it: Sì, ho un libro e un panino.
lines.en: Yes, I’ve got a book and a sandwich.

lessons.title: Tanti!
lessons.subtitle: Plurals
goals: Use the plural articles *i, gli, le*
Spot the nouns that never change

steps.text: One, two, many
Italian makes plurals by changing the last vowel. There are three main patterns.
The: i, gli, le

steps.label: Spelling
steps.text: Some words add an *h* to keep a hard sound: *amica*, *amiche*. But *amico* becomes *amici*, and the *c* goes soft, like the “ch” in “cheese”.

steps.why: Masculine nouns starting with a vowel take *gli*. *I amici* is one of the most common learner mistakes.

steps.text: Words that never change
Some nouns stay the same in the plural. Only the article shows there’s more than one.

steps.why: *Caffè* ends in an accented vowel, so it never changes.

steps.text: In conversation
Five friends walk into a bar. Paolo goes to the counter and orders for everyone.

lines.en: Good morning, guys! What can I get you?

lines.it: Buongiorno! Tre caffè e due cappuccini, per favore.
lines.en: Good morning! Three coffees and two cappuccinos, please.
wrong: Buongiorno! Tre caffèi e due cappuccini, per favore.
Buongiorno! Tre caffè e due cappuccino, per favore.

lines.it: Sì, due cornetti e un panino.
lines.en: Yes, two croissants and a sandwich.
wrong: Sì, due cornette e un panino.
Sì, due cornetti e uno panino.

lines.it: Ecco i cornetti e il panino.
lines.en: Here are the croissants and the sandwich.
Here you are. Thanks a lot!

lessons.title: La mia famiglia
lessons.subtitle: Family and avere
goals: Name the people in your family

steps.text: The family

steps.label: False friend
steps.text: *I parenti* means relatives, not parents. Your parents are *i genitori*. At home you’ll also hear *mamma* and *papà*.
Avere: to have
In lesson 6 you used *ho, hai, ha* for age. Here is the whole verb.

steps.label: Spelling
steps.text: The *h* is silent: *hanno* sounds just like *anno* (year).

steps.it: Ho due fratelli e una sorella.
steps.en: I have two brothers and a sister.

steps.why: *Hanno* is “they have”. *Sono un gatto* would mean “They are a cat”!

steps.prompt: To two friends: “Do you have brothers?”
steps.why: Talking to more than one person is *voi*, so *avete*.

steps.text: My and your
*Mio* (my) and *tuo* (your) agree with the person or thing you have, not with you. A man talking about his sister says *mia sorella*.

steps.label: Rule
steps.text: With one family member, drop the article: *mia madre*, not *la mia madre*. Keep it in the plural (*i miei fratelli*) and with *famiglia* (*la mia famiglia*).

steps.why: *Sorella* is feminine, so *mia*, even though Paolo is a man.
In the plural the article comes back: *i miei*.

steps.text: In conversation
Chiara shows her new flatmate Ben a photo on her phone. One new word: *chi*, “who”.

lines.en: And him? Is that your father?

lines.it: Sì, ho due fratelli. E tu?
lines.en: Yes, I have two brothers. And you?
wrong: Sì, hanno due fratelli. E tu?
Sì, ho due fratello. E tu?

lines.it: Io no. Ma ho tre sorelle!
lines.en: Not me. But I have three sisters!

lessons.title: Com’è?
lessons.subtitle: Describing with adjectives
goals: Make adjectives agree with the noun
Put the adjective in the right place

steps.text: Describing words

steps.en: What’s it like? / What’s he / she like?
steps.note: *Come* + *è*, joined.

steps.text: Four endings, or two
Adjectives agree with their noun: masculine or feminine, singular or plural. Adjectives ending in *-o* have four forms. Those ending in *-e* have only two.

steps.why: Masculine plural: *-i*. The *c* goes soft, just like *amico*, *amici*.

steps.text: Where it goes
Most adjectives come after the noun: *una casa grande*, *un libro interessante*. For “very”, put *molto* in front of the adjective.

steps.it: La mia casa è piccola ma bella.
steps.en: My house is small but beautiful.

steps.label: Heads-up
steps.text: A few common adjectives can go first, and sometimes the meaning shifts: *un uomo grande* is a big man, *un grande uomo* a great man. *Bello* in front changes like an article (*un bel libro*). Just recognise these for now.

steps.why: Feminine plural *vecchie*, and *molto* goes before the adjective.

steps.text: In conversation
Sofia has just moved to Turin (*Torino*). Her friend Luca calls to ask how it’s going. New word: *la coinquilina*, “flatmate” (a woman).

lines.it: Ciao, Sofia! Com’è la casa nuova?
lines.en: Hi, Sofia! What’s the new place like?
And your flatmate? What’s she like?

lines.it: Sì, sono molto felice. Ma sono stanca!
lines.en: Yes, I’m very happy. But I’m tired!
wrong: Sì, sono molto felica. Ma sono stanca!
Sì, ho molto felice. Ma sono stanca!

steps.text: The tens

steps.title: Tap a number to hear it

steps.label: Pattern
steps.text: From *quaranta* on, the tens end in *-anta*. *Sessanta* (60) and *settanta* (70) sound alike, so listen for *-ss-* or *-tt-*.
In between
Join the ten and the unit into one word: *trenta* + *due* = *trentadue*.

steps.title: Tap a number to hear it

steps.label: Two rules
steps.text: Before *uno* and *otto*, the ten drops its last vowel: *ventuno*, *ventotto*, *quarantotto*. And *tre* on the end takes an accent: *ventitré*, *trentatré*.

steps.why: Accent on the final *-tré*.

steps.text: Prices
Prices are euros *e* cents: €3.50 is *tre euro e cinquanta*. In quick speech *euro* is often dropped: *tre e cinquanta*.

steps.note: For more than one thing: *Quanto costano?*

steps.text: In conversation
Saturday morning at a market in Bologna. Emma buys fruit from Gino’s stall. New words: *la mela* (apple), *l’arancia* (orange), and *allora* (so, well then).

lines.en: Good morning, ma’am! What can I get you?
Good morning! How much are the apples?
wrong: Buongiorno! Quanti anni hanno le mele?

lines.it: Due euro e quaranta al chilo.
Un chilo di mele, per favore.
wrong: Uno chilo di mele, per favore.

lines.it: Allora… sono cinque euro e novanta.

steps.text: What time is it?

steps.note: You’ll also hear *Che ora è?* Both are fine.
Literally “they are the three (hours)”: plural, because it’s more than one hour.
One hour is singular: *è l’una*, never *sono le una*.

steps.text: Quarters and halves

items.it: Sono le tre e un quarto.
Sono le quattro meno un quarto.

steps.label: Pattern
steps.text: Add minutes with *e* (and). Take them away from the next hour with *meno* (minus).

steps.why: Quarter to six: the next hour, minus a quarter. (*Le cinque e quarantacinque* works too.)

steps.text: At what time?

steps.note: *A* + *le* = *alle*. At one is *all’una*; at noon, *a mezzogiorno*.

steps.it: A che ora parte il treno?
steps.en: What time does the train leave?

steps.label: Culture
steps.text: Timetables, shops and tickets use the 24-hour clock: *le venti e trenta* is 8:30 pm. In conversation people usually say *le otto e mezza di sera*.

steps.why: *A* and *le* always join into *alle*.

steps.text: In conversation
Marco calls his friend Elena to plan a day trip to Florence. New words: *parte* (leaves), *arriva* (arrives) and *ci vediamo* (see you).

lines.it: Elena, a che ora parte il treno?
lines.en: Elena, what time does the train leave?
wrong: Elena, che ore sono il treno?
Elena, alle ora parte il treno?

lines.en: So shall we meet at nine?
wrong: Allora ci vediamo a le nove?

lines.it: Alle nove meno un quarto, alla stazione.
lines.en: At quarter to nine, at the station.

lines.it: Perfetto. E a che ora arriva?
lines.en: Perfect. And what time does it arrive?

steps.text: The days of the week

steps.title: Tap a day to hear it

steps.label: Spelling
steps.text: Days and months take a small letter in Italian. The days ending in *-dì* (an old word for “day”) are stressed on the last syllable.

steps.label: On Mondays
steps.text: *Lunedì* means this Monday. *Il lunedì* means every Monday. *Domenica* is the only feminine day: *la domenica*.

steps.prompt: “On Saturdays I go to the seaside.”
steps.why: Every Saturday: *il sabato*. Plain *sabato* means this coming Saturday.

steps.text: Today, tomorrow
Months and dates
For a date, use *il* + the number + the month: *il tre giugno*, *il venticinque dicembre*. The first of the month is special: *il primo* (the first).

steps.it: Il mio compleanno è il tre giugno.
steps.en: My birthday is on the third of June.

steps.note: Literally “How many (days) do we have today?” The easy answer: *Oggi è il tre.*

steps.why: The first is *il primo*. Every other day is a plain number.

options: *Il mio compleanno è il dodici ottobre.*
*Il mio compleanno è il ottobre dodici.*
steps.why: Number first, then the month.

steps.text: In conversation
Anna phones a restaurant to book dinner for her mother’s birthday. New words: *prenotare* (to book), *un tavolo* (a table) and *persone* (people).

lines.it: Buonasera! Vorrei prenotare un tavolo per sabato.
lines.en: Good evening! I’d like to book a table for Saturday.
wrong: Buonasera! Vorrei prenotare un tavolo per il sabato.

lines.en: Saturday the fifteenth? For how many people?

lines.it: Sì, sabato quindici. Per quattro persone.
lines.en: Yes, Saturday the fifteenth. For four people.
wrong: Sì, sabato quindici. Per quattro persona.
Sì, il quindici sabato. Per quattro persone.

lines.it: Alle otto e mezza, per favore.
wrong: A otto e mezza, per favore.
Sono le otto e mezza, per favore.

lines.it: Sì, il compleanno di mia madre!
wrong: Sì, il compleanno di la mia madre!
Sì, il compleanno di mio madre!

lines.en: See you Saturday, then! Good evening.

lessons.title: Ripasso 2
lessons.subtitle: Review: a day out
goals: Order, pay and catch up with a friend at a café
Mix articles, plurals, *avere*, adjectives, numbers and time

steps.text: Things and people
This review mixes all of Unit 2. Nothing new, just practice.

options: *I miei genitori hanno una casa grande.*
*I miei genitori sono una casa grande.*

steps.prompt: At a bar, the polite way to order:

steps.text: Numbers and time
In conversation
Saturday morning. Giulia and Sam, old school friends, meet at a café in Rome for the first time in years. New word: *la lezione*, “class”.

lines.en: Good morning, guys! What can I get you?

lines.it: Per me un cappuccino e un cornetto, per favore.
lines.en: A cappuccino and a croissant for me, please.
wrong: Per me una cappuccino e un cornetto, per favore.
Per te un cappuccino e un cornetto, per favore.

lines.narration: They sit down at a table.

lines.it: E la tua famiglia? Come sta?
lines.en: And your family? How are they?

lines.it: Bene, grazie! Ho una figlia. Ha tre anni.
lines.en: Fine, thanks! I have a daughter. She’s three.
wrong: Bene, grazie! Ho una figlia. È tre anni.
Bene, grazie! Ho uno figlia. Ha tre anni.

lines.it: Stanno bene. Hanno una casa nuova a Napoli.
lines.en: They’re well. They have a new house in Naples.
wrong: Stanno bene. Hanno una casa nuovo a Napoli.
Stanno bene. Sono una casa nuova a Napoli.

lines.it: Oh no, sono le undici e mezza! Ho lezione a mezzogiorno.
lines.en: Oh no, it’s half past eleven! I have class at noon.
Excuse me! How much is it?

lines.it: Ecco cinque euro. Ciao, Giulia! A presto!
lines.en: Here’s five euros. Bye, Giulia! See you soon!
wrong: Ecco quindici euro. Ciao, Giulia! A presto!
Ecco cinque euro. Ciao, Giulia! Piacere!

lessons.title: Parlo italiano
lessons.subtitle: Regular -are verbs
goals: Talk about work, study and where you live
Drop the subject pronoun, the way Italians do

steps.text: One pattern, hundreds of verbs
Most Italian verbs end in *-are*. Take off *-are*, add the endings below, and you can use hundreds of verbs, starting with *parlare* (to speak).

steps.label: Pattern
steps.text: The endings are *-o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano*. Every regular *-are* verb uses them.

steps.why: *Noi* always ends in *-iamo*, whatever the verb.

steps.text: Leave out io, tu, lui…
The ending already says who is doing it, so Italians usually drop the pronoun: *Parlo italiano* rather than *Io parlo italiano*. Keep the pronoun for emphasis or contrast: *Io lavoro, tu no!*

steps.label: Pronunciation
steps.text: The *loro* form keeps the stress of the *lui* form: *PAR-la*, *PAR-la-no*; *la-VO-ra*, *la-VO-ra-no*. It never falls on the *-a-* of *-ano*.
Useful -are verbs

steps.label: Spelling
steps.text: Verbs ending in *-iare* keep only one *i*: *mangiare*, *tu mangi*; *studiare*, *tu studi* (never *mangii*). Verbs in *-care* and *-gare* add an *h* to keep the hard sound: *pagare*, *tu paghi*.

steps.prompt: To two friends: “Do you study Italian?”
steps.why: Talking to more than one person is *voi*: *-ate*.

steps.text: In conversation
Luca meets Anna, a new colleague, at the coffee machine. New word: *l’ufficio*, “the office”.

lines.it: Ciao! Sei nuova? Come ti chiami?
lines.en: Hi! Are you new? What’s your name?

lines.it: Sì, mi chiamo Anna. Lavoro in questo ufficio.
lines.en: Yes, my name’s Anna. I work in this office.
wrong: Sì, mi chiamo Anna. Lavora in questo ufficio.
Sì, mi chiamo Anna. Lavoro in questa ufficio.

lines.en: Nice to meet you! Do you live in Milan?

lines.it: No, abito a Monza, ma studio a Milano la sera.
lines.en: No, I live in Monza, but I study in Milan in the evenings.
wrong: No, abita a Monza, ma studia a Milano la sera.
No, abito a Monza, ma studo a Milano la sera.

lines.it: Studio inglese. E tu, parli inglese?
lines.en: I study English. And you, do you speak English?
wrong: Studi inglese. E tu, parli inglese?
Studio inglese. E tu, parla inglese?

lines.it: Sì, parlo inglese. Mangiamo insieme oggi?
lines.en: Yes, I speak English. Shall we eat together today?

lessons.title: Leggo e scrivo
lessons.subtitle: Regular -ere verbs
goals: Use *prendere* for food, drink and transport

steps.text: The -ere pattern
The second group ends in *-ere*. The endings match *-are* except in three places: *lui* ends in *-e*, *voi* in *-ete* and *loro* in *-ono*.

steps.why: *-ere* verbs make *voi* with *-ete*.

steps.text: Useful -ere verbs

steps.label: Pronunciation
steps.text: *Gg* and *c* change sound with the vowel after them. In *leggere* the *gg* is soft, like the “dg” in “edge”. In *leggo* it’s hard, like “leg-go”.
Prendere: take, have, catch
*Prendere* does far more work than “take”. Italians use it to order food and drink, and to catch buses and trains.

steps.prompt: At a bar: “I’ll have a tea.”
steps.why: To order, say *prendo* (I take). *Ho un tè* means you already have one.

steps.text: In conversation
Carla asks Giorgio about his Sunday. New words: *il giornale* (the newspaper) and *anche a te* (you too).

lines.en: What are you doing on Sunday?

lines.it: Leggo il giornale e scrivo a mia madre.
lines.en: I’ll read the paper and write to my mother.
wrong: Leggio il giornale e scrivo a mia madre.
Legge il giornale e scrive a mia madre.

lines.it: Sì! Prendiamo un caffè insieme la sera.
lines.en: Yes! We’re having a coffee together in the evening.
wrong: Sì! Prendete un caffè insieme la sera.
Sì! Abbiamo un caffè insieme la sera.

lines.it: Vive a Firenze. Prendo il treno.
lines.en: He lives in Florence. I’m taking the train.
wrong: Vivo a Firenze. Prendo il treno.
Vive a Firenze. Prende il treno.

lines.en: How nice! Have a good Sunday!

lessons.title: Dormo e capisco
lessons.subtitle: The two -ire patterns
goals: Talk about sleeping, leaving and finishing

steps.text: The -ire pattern
Verbs in *-ire* take the same endings as *-ere*, except *voi*, which ends in *-ite*.
The -isc- verbs
Many *-ire* verbs add *-isc-* before the ending in every form except *noi* and *voi*. Nothing in the infinitive tells you which verbs do this, so learn each one with its *io* form.

steps.label: Pronunciation
steps.text: *-sco* is hard, like “sko”. *-sci* and *-sce* are soft, like “shee” and “sheh”: *capisco* (ca-PEE-sko), *capisci* (ca-PEE-shee).

steps.why: *Capire* takes *-isc-*: *capisco*. (*Capo* means “boss”!)
*Noi* and *voi* never take *-isc-*.

steps.prompt: To two friends: “Do you prefer tea?”
steps.why: *Voi* has no *-isc-*: *preferite*.

steps.text: In conversation
Flatmates Sara and Marco plan the next day. New words: *presto* (early) and *finire di lavorare* (to finish work).

lines.en: What time are you leaving tomorrow?
I leave at eight. And you?

lines.it: Io alle nove. A che ora finisci di lavorare?
lines.en: At nine. What time do you finish work?
So shall we eat together at seven?

lines.it: Sì! Ma stasera dormo presto, sono stanco.
lines.en: Yes! But tonight I’m going to bed early, I’m tired.
wrong: Sì! Ma stasera dorme presto, sono stanco.
Sì! Ma stasera dormisco presto, sono stanco.

steps.text: The verbs that break the rules
The verbs people use most are the ones that don’t follow the patterns. Learn these six as they are.

steps.label: Pattern
steps.text: *Noi* and *voi* are often regular (*andiamo, andate*), while the other forms change completely.

steps.prompt: To a friend: “What are you doing?”

steps.text: Coming and going out

steps.label: Watch out
steps.text: *Uscire* changes its first letter: *esco*, *esci*, *esce*, *escono*, but *usciamo* and *uscite*.
Drinking and saying
Everyday phrases with fare

steps.label: Tip
steps.text: The weather uses *fare*, not *essere*: *fa caldo*, never *è caldo*. And *andare a* + a place or a verb: *vado a Roma*, *vado a mangiare*.
In conversation
Friday afternoon. Giulia texts her friend Paolo about the weekend.

lines.en: What are you doing on Saturday?

lines.it: Vado al mare con mia sorella. Vieni?
lines.en: I’m going to the seaside with my sister. Are you coming?
wrong: Ando al mare con mia sorella. Vieni?
Vado al mare con mia sorella. Vengo?

lines.it: Sì, vengo! A che ora uscite?
lines.en: Yes, I’m coming! What time are you leaving?

lessons.title: Domande
lessons.subtitle: Question words
goals: Ask open questions: who, what, where, when, why, how

steps.text: Question words

steps.label: Word order
steps.text: The question word goes first, and the rest keeps normal order: *Dove abiti?* A subject often moves to the end: *Quando arriva il treno?*

steps.prompt: You want to know where the pharmacy is:

steps.text: Why? Because!

steps.note: The same word means “because”: *Perché studi italiano? — Perché mi piace.*

steps.it: Perché non vieni? — Perché sono stanco.
steps.en: Why aren’t you coming? — Because I’m tired.

steps.text: How much, how many

items.en: How many sisters do you have?

steps.label: Agreement
steps.text: *Quanto* works like an adjective: *quanto* and *quanta* in the singular, *quanti* and *quante* in the plural, matching the noun that follows.

steps.why: *Anni* is masculine plural, so *quanti*.

steps.text: Which one?

steps.note: *Quale* drops its *e* before *è*, with no apostrophe.

options: *Qual è il tuo numero di telefono?*
*Che è il tuo numero di telefono?*
steps.why: No apostrophe: *qual è*. Plenty of Italians get this wrong too.

steps.text: In conversation
Tom has just moved in, and his neighbour Elena shows him around. He has lots of questions. New words: *il mercato* (the market) and *tutti i giorni* (every day).

lines.it: Scusa, chi è il signore con il cane?
lines.en: Sorry, who’s the man with the dog?
wrong: Scusa, che cosa è il signore con il cane?
Scusa, dove è il signore con il cane?

lines.it: È il signor Rossi. È molto simpatico.
lines.en: That’s Mr Rossi. He’s very nice.
Where do you do your shopping?
At the market, in the square.

lines.it: Tutti i giorni, dalle otto all’una.
lines.en: Every day, from eight to one.
And how much are the apples?

lines.it: Due euro al chilo. Perché? Ti piacciono le mele?
lines.en: Two euros a kilo. Why? Do you like apples?

lessons.title: Dov’è…?
lessons.subtitle: Directions and places
goals: Ask where something is and understand the answer
Follow directions: *a destra, a sinistra, dritto*

steps.text: Asking the way

steps.note: *Dove* + *è* = *dov’è*. For more than one thing: *Dove sono…?*

steps.it: Scusi, c’è una farmacia qui vicino?
steps.en: Excuse me, is there a pharmacy near here?

steps.text: C’è or ci sono?

steps.it: Ci sono due farmacie in questa strada.
steps.en: There are two pharmacies on this street.

steps.text: Where things are

steps.label: Tip
steps.text: *A* and *da* join the article after them: *vicino alla stazione*, *di fronte al parco*, *lontano dal centro*. Learn them as phrases for now; lesson 27 has the full table.

steps.prompt: “The bar is next to the bank.”
options: *Il bar è accanto a la banca.*

steps.text: Following directions
Strangers give directions with the polite *Lei* command form. You don’t need to make these yet, just recognise them.

items.en: Take the first on the left.

steps.label: Culture
steps.text: Italians give directions by landmarks more than street names: *dopo la chiesa*, *al semaforo*, *in fondo alla strada*.

steps.prompt: *Giri a sinistra al semaforo.* What do you do?
options: Turn left at the traffic light
Turn right at the traffic light
Go straight past the traffic light

steps.prompt: *È lontano? — No, sono cinque minuti a piedi.*
options: You need to take a bus

steps.text: In conversation
Tom is in Rome and needs a pharmacy. He stops a woman in the street.

lines.it: Scusi, c’è una farmacia qui vicino?
lines.en: Excuse me, is there a pharmacy near here?
wrong: Scusi, ci sono una farmacia qui vicino?
Scusa, c’è una farmacia qui vicino?

lines.it: Sì, non è lontano. Vada dritto e al semaforo giri a destra.
lines.en: Yes, it’s not far. Go straight on and turn right at the traffic light.

lines.it: Al semaforo a destra. E poi?
lines.en: Right at the traffic light. And then?
wrong: Al semaforo a sinistra. E poi?

lines.it: La farmacia è accanto alla banca, di fronte al parco.
lines.en: The pharmacy is next to the bank, opposite the park.
Next to the bank. Thanks so much!

lines.it: Prego! Sono cinque minuti a piedi.
lines.en: You’re welcome! It’s a five-minute walk.

steps.text: Later, Tom texts his friend Luca, who lives in Rome. New word: *subito*, “right away”.

lines.it: Sono in piazza, di fronte alla chiesa.
lines.en: I’m in the square, opposite the church.
wrong: Sono in piazza, di fronte la chiesa.
C’è in piazza, di fronte alla chiesa.

lines.it: Ah, vicino! C’è un bar all’angolo?
lines.en: Oh, that’s close! Is there a café on the corner?

lessons.title: Al ristorante
lessons.subtitle: Eating out
goals: Book a table and order a full meal
Ask for the bill and pay

steps.text: Booking and arriving

steps.it: Ho prenotato un tavolo per due.
steps.en: I’ve booked a table for two.
steps.note: Without a booking: *Avete un tavolo per due?*

steps.text: The courses

items.en: first course: pasta, risotto or soup

steps.label: Culture
steps.text: Nobody expects you to order every course. A *primo* alone, or a *secondo* with a *contorno*, is completely normal. Pasta is a course of its own, never a side dish.
Ordering

steps.note: From lesson 8. *Come primo…* and *come secondo…* (for the first / main course) work too.

steps.en: For the main course I’ll have fish.

steps.prompt: The waiter asks what you’d like. “The chicken for me”:
steps.why: *Per me* is for ordering. *A me* is for likes, in the next lesson.

steps.text: Allergies

steps.note: Men say *allergico*, women *allergica*. *A* joins the article: *alle noci*, *al glutine*.

steps.text: The bill

steps.label: Culture
steps.text: The waiter won’t bring the bill until you ask for it: rushing you would be rude. A *coperto* (cover charge, for bread and service) on the bill is normal. Tipping is optional, and rounding up is plenty.
In conversation
Anna arrives at a *trattoria*, a simple family-run restaurant, for dinner.

lines.en: Good evening! Do you have a booking?

lines.it: Sì, ho prenotato un tavolo per due. Anna Neri.
lines.en: Yes, I’ve booked a table for two. Anna Neri.
wrong: Sì, ho prenotato un tavolo per due. Arrivederci!
No, ho prenotato un tavolo per due.

lines.en: Thank you. What do you recommend?

lines.it: Gli spaghetti al pomodoro sono molto buoni.
lines.en: The spaghetti with tomato sauce is very good.

lines.it: Allora per me gli spaghetti. Ma sono allergica alle noci.
lines.en: Then the spaghetti for me. But I’m allergic to nuts.
wrong: Allora per me gli spaghetti. Ma sono allergico alle noci.
Allora a me gli spaghetti. Ma sono allergica alle noci.

lines.it: Nessun problema, non ci sono noci.
lines.en: No problem, there are no nuts.

lines.it: Il conto, per favore. Possiamo pagare con la carta?
lines.en: The bill, please. Can we pay by card?
wrong: Il conto, prego. Possiamo pagare con la carta?
Il conto, per favore. Possiamo pagare con il carta?

lessons.title: Mi piace!
lessons.subtitle: Likes and preferences
goals: Say what you like and don’t like
Agree and disagree: *anche a me*, *a me no*

steps.text: I like it
Remember *piacere* from lesson 2? It means “to please”. In Italian you don’t like things: things please you. *Mi piace la pizza* is literally “pizza pleases me”.

steps.note: With one thing or a verb: *Mi piace la pizza. Mi piace viaggiare.*
With plural things: *Mi piacciono i gatti.*

steps.why: *Gatti* is plural, so *piacciono*. *Io piaccio* would mean “I am pleasing”!
A verb always takes the singular *piace*.

steps.text: You, him, her

steps.label: Tip
steps.text: *Non* goes first: *Non mi piace il pesce.*

steps.prompt: To a friend: “Do you like Italian music?”

steps.text: Me too, me neither

steps.label: Watch out
steps.text: Because the verb is *piacere*, “me too” is *anche a me*, not *anche io*. Use *anche io* with other verbs: *Studio italiano. — Anche io!*

steps.prompt: *Mi piace il calcio!* You like it too:
*Non mi piace il pesce.* You don’t like it either:

steps.text: Preferring

steps.note: From lesson 19. *Preferisco il tè al caffè*: I prefer tea to coffee.
*Che cosa ti piace di più?* What do you like more?

steps.text: In conversation
Friday night. Chiara and Ben are deciding what to do.

lines.it: Sì, mi piace molto! E a te?
lines.en: Yes, I like it a lot! And you?
wrong: Sì, mi piacciono molto! E a te?
Sì, mi piace molto! E tu?

lines.it: Anche a me! Ti piacciono i film italiani?
lines.en: Me too! Do you like Italian films?

lines.it: Sì, ma preferisco i film americani.
lines.en: Yes, but I prefer American films.
wrong: Sì, ma preferiscono i film americani.
Sì, ma prefero i film americani.

lines.it: Io no, preferisco i film italiani. Allora… pizza?
lines.en: Not me, I prefer Italian films. So… pizza?

lessons.title: Ripasso 3
lessons.subtitle: Review: a weekend in Rome
goals: Get around a city, eat out and talk about likes
Mix all three verb groups and the irregular verbs

steps.text: Verbs
This review mixes all of Unit 3. Nothing new, just practice.
Questions, places, likes
In conversation
Tom’s first evening in Rome, from the station to dinner with his friend Luca. New words: *la carbonara* (a Roman pasta dish) and *buonissimo* (really good).

lines.narration: Tom arrives at the station and looks for Luca’s favourite trattoria.

lines.it: Scusi, c’è una trattoria qui vicino? Si chiama Da Gino.
lines.en: Excuse me, is there a trattoria near here? It’s called Da Gino.
wrong: Scusa, c’è una trattoria qui vicino? Si chiama Da Gino.
Scusi, ci sono una trattoria qui vicino? Si chiama Da Gino.

lines.it: Sì, non è lontano. Vada dritto e prenda la seconda a sinistra.
lines.en: Yes, it’s not far. Go straight on and take the second on the left.
The second on the left. Thanks!

lines.narration: At the trattoria, Luca is already at a table.

lines.it: Tom! Come stai? Che cosa prendi?
lines.en: Tom! How are you? What are you having?

lines.it: La carbonara è buonissima. Ti piace la pasta?
lines.en: The carbonara is really good. Do you like pasta?
Yes, I like it a lot!
Good evening! What are you having?

lines.it: Per me la carbonara, per favore.
wrong: A me la carbonara, per favore.

lines.it: Anche per me. E due acque.
lines.en: Same for me. And two waters.
So, what are you doing tomorrow?

lines.it: Vado al Colosseo. Vieni con me?
lines.en: I’m going to the Colosseum. Are you coming with me?
wrong: Ando al Colosseo. Vieni con me?
Vado al Colosseo. Vengo con me?

lines.it: Sì, vengo! A che ora esci?
lines.en: Yes, I’ll come! What time are you going out?
